endorsements.quote: A pragmatic model is to begin with low-stakes pilots in one or two activities, prespecify local evaluation indicators, review unintended consequences; and scale only after governance, faculty capacity, and equity safeguards are in place [ 6 7 25 33 ].

A pragmatic model is to begin with low-stakes pilots in one or two activities, prespecify local evaluation indicators, review unintended consequences; and scale only after governance, faculty capacity, and equity safeguards are in place [ 6 7 25 33 ].
Institutions should specify which AI tools are approved, what data may be entered, who can access learner outputs, and how long learner data are retained.

Learners should be able to question AI-generated feedback and request human review when AI-derived evidence is discussed in assessment meetings because trust in AI-supported systems depends on whether users can understand, contest, and contextualize AI outputs [ 14 30 31 ].
Therefore, AI-assisted formative assessment activities should require learners to verify AI claims against clinical guidelines, local protocols, patient context, and faculty judgment.

Institutions should also monitor whether AI feedback performs differently across learner characteristics such as language background, disability, gender, race, socioeconomic status, prior digital experience, or familiarity with prompt-based tools [ 7 10 ].

Students should be taught how to formulate prompts, judge the plausibility of AI-generated feedback, verify sources, recognize hallucinations, manage uncertainty, and translate feedback into learning plans.

Before scaling, local pilots should prespecify a small evaluation set, such as learner participation, quality of action plans, change between repeated attempts, quality of dialogue between faculty and learners, learner trust, faculty time burden, equity of access, and unintended effects on assessment culture.

Educators need sufficient AI literacy to select tools that fit learning outcomes, recognize limitations in AI outputs, and help learners interpret feedback in relation to clinical reasoning and professional values [ 9 25 32 ].
Require transparent criteria, human review, and an appeal process for any higher-stakes use.

unlisted_practices: Provide students with access to approved AI tools rather than leaving them to purchase or select AI systems individually when AI-assisted formative assessment is part of the formal curriculum.
Explicitly define the boundary between formative and summative use of AI-generated evidence.
Prohibit entry of identifiable patient data into unapproved or public AI tools.
Evaluate AI-assisted formative assessment on educational outcomes rather than technology adoption metrics such as prompts submitted or dashboard views.
Design AI-assisted formative activities so each ends with one or two specific learner actions rather than a long list of AI-generated observations.
Begin AI implementation from the curriculum problem and learning outcome rather than from the AI tool.
Clarify whether vendors may use submitted data for model training.
Do not let AI ratings replace faculty, standardized patient, or patient ratings in communication skills assessment.
